StringWithMarkup.String: /LABORATORY ANIMALS: Acute Exposure/ The alkylating properties of trichlorphone and butonate towards N-7 of guanine  of nucleic acids was studied in-vivo in mice.  Male mice were given 160 milligrams per kilogram (mg/kg) trichlorphone or 5 or 10 mg/kg butonate intraperitoneally.  Both compounds were labeled with carbon-14 in the OCH3 positions.  Animals were killed and nucleic acids were isolated from different organs.  The nucleic acids and urine from the animals were analyzed for 7-methylguanine labeled with carbon-14.  The excretion rate was determined by killing animals at intervals up to 24 hours.  The amounts of 7-methylguanine excreted in urine were used to compare the methylating capacity of butonate and trichlorphone with known data for dichlorvos.  Maximum amounts of radiocarbon in 7-methylguanine were found in lungs, kidneys and testicles, as well as in livers.  These amounts were found shortly after killing and rapidly decreased with time.  The excretion rate of 7-methylguanine was very rapid.  For butonate the half life in liver was about 2 hours.  In the whole body the half life of trichlorphone was less than 24 hours.  Based on the excretion of 7-methylguanine in urine, the methylating capacity towards N-7 of guanine in nucleic acids was represented by a ratio of about 100:10:25 for dichlorvos, butonate and trichlorphone, respectively.  The authors conclude that the methylating capacity of butonate is lower than that of trichlorphone as shown in-vivo, and is in agreement with the steric factors, the lipid/water partition and the rate of breakdown in the body.

StringWithMarkup.String: Butonate's former production and use as an insecticide may have resulted in its direct release to the environment. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 1.1X10-4 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates butonate will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the atmosphere. Vapor-phase butonate will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 4.3 days. Particulate-phase butonate will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. Butonate is susceptible to direct photolysis by sunlight and the photolysis products of an aqueous solution of butonate exposed to UV light were found to be vinyl butonate, chlorophos, DDVP, and HCl. If released to soil, butonate is expected to have low mobility based upon an estimated Koc of 1,100. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 3.0X10-10 atm-cu m/mole. Butonate is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces based upon its vapor pressure. If released into water, butonate is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the estimated Koc. Volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. An estimated BCF of 4.1 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. A base-catalyzed second-order hydrolysis rate constant of 4.7X10-2 L/mole-sec(SRC) was estimated for butonate; this corresponds to half-lives of 4.7 years, 170 days, and 17 days at pH values of 7, 8, and 9, respectively. In an aqueous environment hydrolysis study, butonate was found to hydrolyze to the hydroxy deriviative chlorophos in acid media (pH 1.9 to 5) and dehydrochlorination occurred in alkaline media (pH 7.4 to 9.4) to produce vinyl butonate. Occupational exposure and general population exposure should be low or non-existent since butonate is no longer produced or used in the US. In the past, butonate was applied directly to the environment as an insecticide and exposure to this compound was primarily in the field where it was applied. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.
